Here are the draft order standings for the 1964 season based off of the salaries and wins from the 1963 season.



Google sheet for Draft formula



For those new to this formula, or that have forgotten, we take a snapshot of the teams salaries every 20 games, and based on that, calculate how many wins a team should be expected to win. Then, from that expectation, the draft order for the first round is determined by the score a team gets. Essentially how much better a team did than expected. So the higher your score the better.



There is also a column in the charts for Target Wins (Discussed more thoroughly below). For reference sake, I will be using a score of 20 as the target goal.



The (new) formula:

TeamSal= Each team's salary averaged out over 9 snapshots across the season



TILAS= Team Independent League Average Salary (i.e., the league average salary minus the team in question) averaged over 9 snapshots across the season.


TIDAS= Team Independent Division Average Salary (i.e., the division average salary minus the team in question) averaged over 9 snapshots across the season.



DivSal= Average salary for the teams in the opposing division of the team in question's league averaged over 9 snapshots across the season.



XTILAS= Team Independent League Average Salary for the interleague opponent that the team in question plays more frequently.



OppSal= Salary of the interleague opponent that the team in question plays more frequently averaged over 9 snapshots across the season.


(%)= ((((TIDAS*(60/162))+(DivSal*(60/162))+(OppSal*(6/162))+XTILAS*(36/162)))-TeamSal)/TILAS)


AcW= each team's actual wins during the season


ExpW= ((81*-(%)+81)


AdjW= (AcW*Multiplier)


TrgtW= (ExpW+(ExpW/Multiplier))


Score= ((((AdjW-ExpW)/AdjW)*100))


And, as the season goes on and the actual wins start to add up, the numbers start to reach the positive side of the spectrum. Once we get to the 20 game mark I'll add a post for projections which gives a better idea of the actual standings than the raw standings alone -- though isn't entirely accurate as salaries and wins change frequently... it gets more accurate as the season progresses.



*As a reminder, the salary used in the Score formula is a combination of the TeamSal and the TILAS from the Season Salary chart.

author: chargingryno
own:
I definitely see the side of wanting owners to make keeper lists strategic. As a commish, the thing I worry about most is making sure that teams who need the most help are able to get it. This is good for league parity as well as owner retention. 



I think if you limit it to 1 drop/pickup per owner, that would limit the chaos and also allow owners who need a little more at the end get the help they need, while still making the keeper list 



The way I envision it, it'd be first come, first served within a 24hr period. Each owner only gets 1 drop/pickup before their roster is final. If I drop player A and pick up player B, and someone else later on picks up player A and drops player C, I am NOT able to drop player D and pick up player C as my drop/pickup was already made.

The way I see it, how we handle future drafts can be determined by how we handle the # of protected players. 



If we only get to protect 5-7 players, I don't see a reason for giving the expansion teams top picks in future drafts given the nature of the formula. 



If we set protected players at 9-12, then I think you have to give the expansion teams top picks for the next 2-3 seasons in order to give then a chance at competing within the next 10 years. 



So that's something to consider as well.

Here are the draft order standings for the 1969 draft based off of the salaries and wins from the 1968 season.



Google sheet for Draft formula



For those new to this formula, or that have forgotten, we take a snapshot of the teams salaries every 20 games, and based on that, calculate how many wins a team should be expected to win. Then, from that expectation, the draft order for the first round is determined by the score a team gets. Essentially how much better a team did than expected. So the higher your score the better.



There is also a column in the charts for Target Wins (Discussed more thoroughly below). For reference sake, I will be using a score of 20 as the target goal.



The (new) formula:

TeamSal= Each team's salary averaged out over 9 snapshots across the season



TILAS= Team Independent League Average Salary (i.e., the league average salary minus the team in question) averaged over 9 snapshots across the season.


TIDAS= Team Independent Division Average Salary (i.e., the division average salary minus the team in question) averaged over 9 snapshots across the season.



DivSal= Average salary for the teams in the opposing division of the team in question's league averaged over 9 snapshots across the season.



XTILAS= Team Independent League Average Salary for the interleague opponent that the team in question plays more frequently.



OppSal= Salary of the interleague opponent that the team in question plays more frequently averaged over 9 snapshots across the season.


(%)= ((((TIDAS*(60/162))+(DivSal*(60/162))+(OppSal*(6/162))+XTILAS*(36/162)))-TeamSal)/TILAS)


AcW= each team's actual wins during the season


ExpW= ((81*-(%)+81)


AdjW= (AcW*Multiplier)


TrgtW= (ExpW+(ExpW/Multiplier))


Score= ((((AdjW-ExpW)/AdjW)*100))


And, as the season goes on and the actual wins start to add up, the numbers start to reach the positive side of the spectrum. Once we get to the 20 game mark I'll add a post for projections which gives a better idea of the actual standings than the raw standings alone -- though isn't entirely accurate as salaries and wins change frequently... it gets more accurate as the season progresses.



*As a reminder, the salary used in the Score formula is a combination of the TeamSal and the TILAS from the Season Salary chart.

I’ll play devils advocate and put out a scenario that I fear in my head and also that another owner has shared as happening in a league that didn’t have rules connecting the picks to keepers.



Let’s so going into the 69 season a team has 25 keepers. All They really need is one good pitcher so Team trades 1-10 picks all for one star player. All those picks were useless to the owner as they had 25 already, and then were able to trade them all for a major upgrade. 



I think of it almost like a salary cap. In RL, you can’t just trade Joe Smith for mike Jones without also considering that Smith makes $10m/y and Jones makes $20m. If teams want to take that salary then they can, but it’s some they have to consider. The same thing goes for picks in my mind. If I trade my 6th round pick, I do so with the knowledge that it means I have to cut 6 players. This season, chrondon it’s different cause you weren’t planning to do so, and so cutting 7 guys when you didn’t expect it would have put you and your team in a bad place. But going forward it’s something you can plan for and be able to make the decision on whether it’s worth the cost of the pick. 



Ex. “I can trade my 5th for Joe Smith, but then I’d also have to cut mike Jones, so maybe it’s worth it to just trade my 4th for Smith so I can keep Jones”

author: frazzman80
own:
Thank you so much for putting this together j4m and for facilitating the conversation ryno. There is data that stands out as significant to me and I'd love to get thoughts and opinion on these. I appreciate the caveat of the one "outlier" team that gave up. Is there enough data to just remove that season completely and still have a statistical analysis that works? I'd hate for one extreme to skew the dataset.



1. "Extreme Low" and "Extreme High" - How many teams do these represent? If it's minimal, could we throw these out altogether and focus on the 80-85% of normal teams in the other categories? Also...how many successful "Extreme low" teams started out as a regular "Lowest 25", racked up wins and then dumped a lot of salary to game their SCORE and move up in the draft substatially? How many "Extreme high" teams decided that the quality of players/salary was more important than their draft position and took on salary at the deadline? Can we just exclude these altogether?



2. If we do exclude the "Extreme"s, These are the numbers that concern me...

	
		

			Lowest 25%
			 
			Salary --> Top 25% Pick
			17.24%
		
		

			Mid-Low 25%
			 
			Salary --> Top 25% Pick
			17.24%
		
		

			Mid-High 25%
			 
			Salary --> Top 25% Pick
			31.03%
		
		

			Highest 25%
			 
			Salary --> Top 25% Pick
			34.48%
		
	

In this table, the two bottom tiers have a 13.79 - 17.24% less chance of getting a top 4/5 pick than their higher salaried opponents. This speaks volumes to the problem I originally noted that teams with less talent (salary) have a more difficult time winning enough games to get a good Score than teams with more talent (salary) do. Given a blank slate to setup my team, I'd always choose to have a "Mid-High 25%" or a "Highest 25%" team and get the 31% or 34% chance to get a top 5 pick as opposed to having only a 17.24% chance to get that pick with the lower salary team.



To me, this proves that better talented, higher salaried teams are set up to get the best picks.



3. But it's not just the top 4/5 picks that are skewed to the higher salaried teams. It's also the top half of the draft as well as noted below.

Salaries by Half to Reach Top 50% Pick:


	
		

			Lowest Half
			Salary --> Top 50% Pick
			46.55%
		
		

			Highest Half
			Salary --> Top 50% Pick
			53.45%
		
	

It is significant that in order to get a top 10 pick, a majority of the time all you need to do is have a "Mid-High 25%" or "Highest 25%" salary. If you have a "Lowest 25%" or "Low-Mid 25%" team, over half the time you will have a pick 11-20.



4. Score backs this up.



If you want a positive SCORE, have a Mid-high 25% or Highest 25% salary as noted below.

	
		

			Lowest 25%
			9.22
			-1.19
		
		

			Mid-Low 25%
			9.55
			-3.47
		
		

			Mid-High 25%
			8.70
			0.00
		
		

			Highest 25%
			7.61
			1.00
		
	



5. Performance vs. EW backs this up



If you want to outperform your EW, have a Mid-high 25% or Highest 25% salary as noted below.

	
		

			Lowest 25%
			 
			Salary --> ActW-ExpW
			-29
		
		

			Mid-Low 25%
			 
			Salary --> ActW-ExpW
			-89
		
		

			Mid-High 25%
			 
			Salary --> ActW-ExpW
			-4
		
		

			Highest 25%
			 
			Salary --> ActW-ExpW
			54
		
	



So long as your salary isn't "EXTREMELY high", you will outperform your EW and get a great SCORE!



So in my mind, the data clearly shows that there needs to be something that helps the lower salaried teams.



Yes, the highlighted portions of the formula descriptions help. But they help every team equally who takes them to heart. A team that eschews extra PAs and IP but has a core of $68 million is still going to dramatically perform worse than a team that eschews extra PAs and IP but has a core of $85 million. That "optimized" $85 million team is going to take 2 of 3 (or more) games from that optimized $68 million team EVERY series. High 25% teams will naturally beat Low 25% teams FREQUENTLY. High 25% teams will beat Low-Mid 25% teams FREQUENTLY.



I understand that strength of schedule offsets this and EWs are different from both, but it's alarming to see the average draft position of the bottom 2 tiers at 9.385 (remember, most of this data is from a 16 team draft, so that's IN THE BOTTOM HALF of the draft) vs the 8.155 of the top 2 tiers. If I can put together a team with a "Mid-High 25%" or "High 25%" salary, ON AVERAGE, I will draft 1.23 spots higher than if I have a "Lowest 25%" or "Mid-low" 25% team.



Fixes: Winning above your EW should net you a high pick. I don't want to see teams failing to meet their EW suddenly getting top 3 or top 5 picks. But I still advocate taking adjusted wins into consideration for the SCORE. (Actual wins + Adjusted wins) / 2 and then determining SCORE would bring some balance to this. It would reward lower salaried teams with a "weighted win" boosting up their Score total. The same "weighted win" would prevent high salaried teams from padding their score by beating poor teams over and over and over and normalize their wins (ala WIS using normalization between the seasons/eras). I understand that this may means that a team with a low salary gets a win and it's worth 1.1 wins and a team with a high salary gets a win and it's worth 0.94 wins, but if it helps the lower salaried teams to be more competitive, I'm all for it. I think the league will be better off having multiple viable franchises than 5-8 dynasties.

author: just4me
own:
we've now been using this modified version of the formula for more seasons than the original version. I've run some analytics, but most aren't in easy to present format yet, which I hope to update and share some things over this week. That said, I have a few highlights I thought I'd share:



In short, the boost to lower salary teams has had a slight boost to their picks across the board. Prior to the adjustment the correlation for salary and pick was -0.034, so this change has caused lower salaried teams to draft better on average, while still maintaining the goal of everyone trying to win every game.




There was almost no impact here. The relative strength of a team by salary against their opponents was previously at -0.046, so this small of a change could just be sample size issues in the two data sets, or a small increase in negative correlation to ones strength against the league in acquiring a pick. However, all told, a teams relative strength has almost no impact at all in where it ends up picking, which means any team has a chance at any pick any season.




This is my favorite. On the old version of the formula this was a .714. Basically, by making this adjustment to a teams Exp W, we have increased the accuracy of the Exp W as a predictor of Act W. This went from being able to account for 71% of the variability in wins to now explaining 91% of the variability. Amazingly, if I remove Georgia from the sample, it jumps all the way to 95%. This also helps explain the reason salary has become a negative indicator of draft position as if teams all hit their exp W, it's essentially just inverse salary relative to their schedule (so a few teams slightly shuffled from a raw salary order, but mostly a salary order). That said, the variability here isn't an impactor on the draft pick as the variance from EXp W by Act W could be both better or worse, so this treats a team predicted to win 78 that wins 80 the same as one that won 76, where for draft purposes, the one that won 80 will get a better pick than the one that won 76, which is another reason this doesn't mean as much towards the draft positioning from salary alone. Basically, this just means, that using a schedule-adjusted salary with an adjustment as we're doing accounts for 91-95% of the variance we can see in a teams win spread from the expected wins that formula gives.




Basically, the more wins you get over your expected wins the higher your pick. Or in strict terms, the number of wins relative to your expected wins accounts for 88% of where your pick ends up. Other factors, such as salary, other teams salaries, and their relative wins account for the rest. 




I'll have a few more charts and details over the coming days, but this change appears to have solved the issues we were encountering prior with low salary teams struggling in general to land top pick relative to higher salaried teams.

There is also a column in the charts for Target Wins (Discussed more thoroughly below). For reference sake, I will be using a score of 20 as the target goal.



The (new) formula:

TeamSal= Each team's salary averaged out over 9 snapshots across the season



TILAS= Team Independent League Average Salary (i.e., the league average salary minus the team in question) averaged over 9 snapshots across the season.


TIDAS= Team Independent Division Average Salary (i.e., the division average salary minus the team in question) averaged over 9 snapshots across the season. ***Not currently used in formula



DivSal= Average salary for the teams in the opposing division of the team in question's league averaged over 9 snapshots across the season.



XTILAS= Team Independent League Average Salary for the interleague opponent that the team in question plays more frequently.



OppSal= Salary of the interleague opponent that the team in question plays more frequently averaged over 9 snapshots across the season.


(%)= ((((TIDAS*(60/162))+(DivSal*(60/162))+(OppSal*(6/162))+XTILAS*(36/162)))-TeamSal)/TILAS) ***Not the current formula - will update with current formula


AcW= each team's actual wins during the season


ExpW= ((81*-(%)+81)^(%/-10)+1) ***Updated for 1971 season from  ((81*-(%)+81)


AdjW= (AcW*Multiplier)


TrgtW= (ExpW+(ExpW/Multiplier))


Score= ((((AdjW-ExpW)/AdjW)*100))

We lost the division despite out-scoring Minnesota by 157 runs (while allowing only 28 more).  I don’t want to say it was bad luck (more likely, bad managing!) but our pitching very much under-performed!  We allowed an average of .280, a WHIP of 1.49 and an ERA of 4.89. Tim Raines (5th in AL MVP despite hitting 21 points below his real life avg.)

2B Ryne Sandberg

LF Tim Raines

RF Darryl Strawberry

Tim Raines scored 143 runs (2nd in the league) and now has 914 runs scored in his first 6 seasons - that’s an average of 152.3 runs per season.  He also stole 96 bases, just a base more than his 6-season average of 95.  He is now 8th in league history, but only 120 behind Joe Morgan for 3rd place.  Fernando Valenzuela won 20 games and Charlie Liebrandt won 19 (could have won his 20th on the last game of the season but the bullpen blew it.)



Early in the season we had fallen behind, so I traded for Fred Lynn and Charlie Kerfeld to shore up CF and the bullpen respectively, but it wasn’t enough and cost us our 2nd and 3rd in the upcoming draft.  Going forward, the pitching is going to get worse, while the offense should be even better.  It will depend on competition as to whether we can compete for the division in 87.

author: just4me
own:
Also from an older conversation, discussing the general distribution of picks:



Quote post by just4me on 11/15/2023 8:50:00 PM:

we've now been using this modified version of the formula for more seasons than the original version. I've run some analytics, but most aren't in easy to present format yet, which I hope to update and share some things over this week. That said, I have a few highlights I thought I'd share:



In short, the boost to lower salary teams has had a slight boost to their picks across the board. Prior to the adjustment the correlation for salary and pick was -0.034, so this change has caused lower salaried teams to draft better on average, while still maintaining the goal of everyone trying to win every game.




There was almost no impact here. The relative strength of a team by salary against their opponents was previously at -0.046, so this small of a change could just be sample size issues in the two data sets, or a small increase in negative correlation to ones strength against the league in acquiring a pick. However, all told, a teams relative strength has almost no impact at all in where it ends up picking, which means any team has a chance at any pick any season.




This is my favorite. On the old version of the formula this was a .714. Basically, by making this adjustment to a teams Exp W, we have increased the accuracy of the Exp W as a predictor of Act W. This went from being able to account for 71% of the variability in wins to now explaining 91% of the variability. Amazingly, if I remove Georgia from the sample, it jumps all the way to 95%. This also helps explain the reason salary has become a negative indicator of draft position as if teams all hit their exp W, it's essentially just inverse salary relative to their schedule (so a few teams slightly shuffled from a raw salary order, but mostly a salary order). That said, the variability here isn't an impactor on the draft pick as the variance from EXp W by Act W could be both better or worse, so this treats a team predicted to win 78 that wins 80 the same as one that won 76, where for draft purposes, the one that won 80 will get a better pick than the one that won 76, which is another reason this doesn't mean as much towards the draft positioning from salary alone. Basically, this just means, that using a schedule-adjusted salary with an adjustment as we're doing accounts for 91-95% of the variance we can see in a teams win spread from the expected wins that formula gives.




Basically, the more wins you get over your expected wins the higher your pick. Or in strict terms, the number of wins relative to your expected wins accounts for 88% of where your pick ends up. Other factors, such as salary, other teams salaries, and their relative wins account for the rest.

own:
There’s no desire to adjust the formula as these findings confirmed to me that things are working as intended. 

The formula is designed to prevent tanking by incentivizing winning all season long; while also not disproportionately making it harder for weak teams to be able to rebuild and compete again. It should be possible for high salaried teams to get higher picks. The reason it’s “harder” for high salary teams is because it’s easier to win against lower salaried teams than it is to win against high salaried teams. 



An $85m team going 8-2 against a $60m team isn’t “performing above expectations”. However, a $60m team going 4-6 against said $85m team would be.
